title: The Age-Specific Quantitative Effects of Metabolic Risk Factors on Cardiovascular Diseases and Diabetes: A Pooled Analysis
abstract: BACKGROUND: The effects of systolic blood pressure (SBP), serum total cholesterol (TC), fasting plasma glucose (FPG), and body mass index (BMI) on the risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) have been established in epidemiological studies, but consistent estimates of effect sizes by age and sex are not available. METHODS: We reviewed large cohort pooling projects, evaluating effects of baseline or usual exposure to metabolic risks on ischemic heart disease (IHD), hypertensive heart disease (HHD), stroke, diabetes, and, as relevant selected other CVDs, after adjusting for important confounders. We pooled all data to estimate relative risks (RRs) for each risk factor and examined effect modification by age or other factors, using random effects models. RESULTS: Across all risk factors, an average of 123 cohorts provided data on 1.4 million individuals and 52,000 CVD events. Each metabolic risk factor was robustly related to CVD. At the baseline age of 55-64 years, the RR for 10 mmHg higher SBP was largest for HHD (2.16; 95% CI 2.09-2.24), followed by effects on both stroke subtypes (1.66; 1.39-1.98 for hemorrhagic stroke and 1.63; 1.57-1.69 for ischemic stroke). In the same age group, RRs for 1 mmol/L higher TC were 1.44 (1.29-1.61) for IHD and 1.20 (1.15-1.25) for ischemic stroke. The RRs for 5 kg/m(2) higher BMI for ages 55-64 ranged from 2.32 (2.04-2.63) for diabetes, to 1.44 (1.40-1.48) for IHD. For 1 mmol/L higher FPG, RRs in this age group were 1.18 (1.08-1.29) for IHD and 1.14 (1.01-1.29) for total stroke. For all risk factors, proportional effects declined with age, were generally consistent by sex, and differed by region in only a few age groups for certain risk factor-disease pairs. CONCLUSION: Our results provide robust, comparable and precise estimates of the effects of major metabolic risk factors on CVD and diabetes by age group.

claims.text: At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 10 mmHg higher SBP is 2.16 for hypertensive heart disease.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 10 mmHg higher SBP is 1.66 for hemorrhagic stroke.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 10 mmHg higher SBP is 1.63 for ischemic stroke.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 1 mmol/L higher total cholesterol is 1.44 for ischemic heart disease.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 1 mmol/L higher total cholesterol is 1.20 for ischemic stroke.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 5 kg/m² higher BMI is 2.32 for diabetes.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 5 kg/m² higher BMI is 1.44 for ischemic heart disease.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 1 mmol/L higher fasting plasma glucose is 1.18 for ischemic heart disease.
At baseline age 55-64 years, the relative risk per 1 mmol/L higher fasting plasma glucose is 1.14 for total stroke.
Proportional risk effects of metabolic risk factors on cardiovascular disease and diabetes decline with increasing age.
Proportional risk effects of metabolic risk factors on cardiovascular disease and diabetes are generally consistent by sex.

limitations.text: The pooling studies used in the analysis only covered prospective cohorts from North America, Western Europe, and the Asia-Pacific region.
Some individual cohorts were included in more than one pooling project.
Differences remained in disease outcome definitions, such as evaluating diabetes mortality in PSC versus diabetes incidence in APCSC.
Because evidence was pooled from observational prospective cohort studies, unmeasured and residual confounding cannot be ruled out.
Prior global comparative risk assessment analyses lacked consistent effect size measurements by age, sex, and region.

future_work.text: Conduct periodic and consistent monitoring of population trends and metabolic risk factor effect sizes to prioritize disease prevention programs.

methodologies.name: Random-effects pooled cohort meta-analysis
methodologies.description: Pooled participant-level and cohort-level data across major prospective cohort collaborations using random-effects models and statistical simulations to derive age-stratified relative risks for metabolic risk factors.
